sources.title: Medicinal plants used in Trinidad and Tobago: a TRAMIL-methodology ethnobotanical survey
sources.notes: TRAMIL-methodology survey of 450 households in Trinidad and Tobago. Documents: fevergrass/fever (46 cites), caraille/Momordica/diabetes (7), saffron-hardi/Curcuma/afterbirth (17), ginger/cold & cough (2), aloes/cooling (8), soursop/HBP (8), neem/diabetes (7), gully root/Petiveria/cold & cough (1), breadfruit/HBP (11), passion fruit/P. edulis/HBP (1), barbadine/P. quadrangularis/HBP (9). Guava, hibiscus, moringa, dogwood, Bryophyllum not in this survey.

sources.title: Traditional herbal medicine use in Jamaica: a TRAMIL ethnobotanical survey
sources.notes: TRAMIL survey of Jamaica (J Ethnopharmacol 169:314-327, PMID 25929450). Documents: cerasee/blood cleanse (67 cites), leaf of life/Bryophyllum/cold (51), sinkle bible/Aloe/washout (54), soursop/nerves (83), fever grass/fever (70, TRAMIL-significant), ginger/bellyache (25), guinea hen weed/headache (23).

sources.title: Traditional uses of Psidium guajava for diarrheal disorders: a multi-country review
sources.notes: Review covering 44 countries including Trinidad and Tobago, Cuba, Guadeloupe and Martinique; documents guava leaf use for diarrhea. PMC11377350.

sources.title: Psidium guajava: a review of its traditional uses, phytochemistry and pharmacology
sources.authors: Gutiérrez, R.M.P.; Mitchell, S.; Solis, R.V.
sources.notes: J Ethnopharmacol 117(1):1-27, PMID 18353572. Backup source for guava traditional uses. URL not preserved in working notes.

sources.title: Hibiscus sabdariffa (Roselle) plant profile
sources.notes: Documents the sorrel Christmas drink tradition in Jamaica and folk antihypertensive use; confirms 'sorrel' as the Jamaican name.

sources.title: Moringa oleifera in Jamaica: nutritional and medicinal review
sources.notes: Documents moringa teas, juices and meals in Jamaican households since the 2000s.

sources.title: Petiveria alliacea: TRAMIL study on traditional uses and safety (Costa Rica)
sources.notes: Costa Rican TRAMIL study documenting an abortive effect attributed to Petiveria (uterine smooth-muscle contraction); contraindicated in pregnancy. Corroborated for Jamaica.

sources.title: Momordica charantia for glycemic control: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
sources.notes: 8 RCTs, n=423. FBG -0.85 mmol/L, PPG -2.28 mmol/L, HbA1c -0.38%, total cholesterol -0.38 mmol/L. High heterogeneity; findings conflict with Cochrane review (insufficient evidence) and one 2024 null review. PMID 38784554, PMC11112315.

sources.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of ginger for nausea and vomiting
sources.notes: Nutr J 13:20. 12 RCTs, n=1278. Nausea improved; vomiting not significantly reduced. Low-quality evidence overall; no significant safety signal. PMID 24642205, PMC3995184.

sources.title: Hibiscus sabdariffa for blood pressure: systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.notes: Nutr Rev 80(6):1723-1737. 17 RCTs; systolic BP -7.10 mmHg vs placebo. PMID 34927694, PMC9086798.

sources.title: Efficacy of turmeric extracts and curcumin for alleviating arthritis symptoms: systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Daily, J.W.; Yang, M.; Park, S.
sources.notes: J Med Food 19(8):717-729. 8 RCTs; pain VAS -2.04, WOMAC -15.36. DISCLOSURE: first author affiliated with Daily Manufacturing, Inc. (turmeric supplement manufacturer). PMID 27533649, PMC5003001.

sources.title: Aloe vera for wound healing: review of clinical trials
sources.notes: 23 clinical trials reviewed; supports complementary use of Aloe vera for burn wound healing. PMC6330525, PMID 30666070. URL not preserved in working notes.

sources.title: Annona muricata (soursop): phytochemistry and anticancer potential
sources.notes: Int J Mol Sci 16(7):15625-15658. Anticancer evidence limited to in vitro and animal studies; no human trials.

sources.title: Annonacin neurotoxicity and atypical parkinsonism
sources.notes: PMID 14675150. Annonacin (from Annonaceae, incl. soursop) is neurotoxic; linked to atypical parkinsonism in Guadeloupe. URL not preserved in working notes.

sources.title: Petiveria alliacea in a mouse breast-cancer model
sources.notes: Mouse breast-cancer model study of Petiveria alliacea (accessed via BMC protocol page). Preliminary animal evidence only.

sources.title: Hypotensive and bradycardic effects of Artocarpus altilis leaf extract in rats
sources.notes: PMID 22830437. Aqueous breadfruit leaf extract hypotensive and bradycardic in rats (UWI Mona, Jamaica). Animal evidence only. URL not preserved in working notes.

sources.title: Moringa oleifera: review of safety and efficacy in human studies
sources.notes: PMID 25808883, PMC6680322. 5 human studies; anti-hyperglycemic and anti-dyslipidemic effects; no adverse effects reported. Small studies. URL not preserved in working notes.

sources.title: Kalanchoe pinnata (Bryophyllum pinnatum): phytochemistry and pharmacology review
sources.notes: Review; preclinical wound-healing evidence is the most extensive. Also documents bufadienolides (cardiac-glycoside poisoning risk).

sources.title: Jamaican Dogwood: uses, side effects and safety
sources.notes: States there is no evidence supporting Jamaican dogwood use or any other use in humans (evidence gap explicitly discussed). Documents rotenone-related toxicity risks.

sources.title: Neem oil poisoning: clinical review
sources.notes: PMC9358515. Review of neem oil poisoning, esp. pediatric: hepatic toxicity, encephalopathy, seizures.

sources.title: Anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects of Passiflora edulis leaf extract in mice
sources.notes: Aqueous Passiflora edulis leaf extract showed anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects in mice; notes traditional Brazilian use for anxiety and insomnia. Animal evidence only.

sources.title: Aloe vera: NCCIH herbs at a glance
sources.authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
sources.notes: NCCIH summary: some support for burn/wound healing; aloe latex risks; IARC classifies aloe vera leaf extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans; pregnancy caution.

sources.title: Turmeric: adverse effects information
sources.notes: Documents turmeric adverse effects: gallstone/biliary concerns, liver injury reports, bleeding risk. URL not preserved in working notes.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Leaf tea widely used across the Caribbean to bring down fever; one of the most-cited remedies in Jamaican and Trinidadian ethnobotanical surveys.
plants.disambiguation_note: Fever grass here is Cymbopogon citratus (lemongrass). It is distinct from citronella grasses (Cymbopogon nardus / C. winterianus), which are grown mainly for mosquito-repelling oil and are not the traditional fever remedy.

names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Trinidad and Tobago survey)

names.name: Lemongrass
names.notes: Widely used English name; no island-specific source retrieved

traditional_uses.use: Leaf tea taken to reduce fever

claims.claim: Fever grass leaf tea reduces fever

assessments.summary: Fever use is strongly documented in Caribbean ethnobotanical surveys: 70 citations in the Jamaican TRAMIL survey (TRAMIL-significant) and 46 citations in Trinidad and Tobago.
assessments.population: 450 households (Trinidad and Tobago); Jamaican survey households
assessments.main_findings: Among the most frequently cited fever remedies in both surveys.
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not clinical efficacy against fever.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Bitter vine used in Jamaica as a 'blood cleanser' and in Trinidad and Tobago for diabetes; among the best-known Caribbean bush medicines.
plants.disambiguation_note: Cerasee is Momordica charantia (bitter melon/bitter gourd). The name is sometimes loosely applied to other bitter vines; the TRAMIL surveys identify it as M. charantia.

names.name: Cerasee
names.notes: Picking et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Jamaica survey)

names.name: Caraille
names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Trinidad and Tobago survey)

claims.claim: Cerasee (bitter melon) helps lower blood sugar in diabetes

assessments.summary: A 2024 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (n=423) found bitter melon reduced fasting blood glucose (-0.85 mmol/L), postprandial glucose (-2.28 mmol/L) and HbA1c (-0.38%), but heterogeneity was high and findings conflict with the Cochrane review and a 2024 null review.
assessments.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
assessments.main_findings: FBG -0.85 mmol/L; PPG -2.28 mmol/L; HbA1c -0.38%; total cholesterol -0.38 mmol/L.
assessments.limitations: High heterogeneity; small trials; conflicts with Cochrane (insufficient evidence) and one 2024 null review.

assessments.summary: Use for diabetes documented in the Trinidad and Tobago TRAMIL survey (7 citations).
assessments.main_findings: Caraille/Momordica cited for diabetes (7 citations).
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy.

claims.claim: Cerasee cleanses the blood

assessments.summary: Blood-cleansing use strongly documented in the Jamaican TRAMIL survey (67 citations), one of the highest-cited uses in the survey.
assessments.main_findings: Cerasee cited 67 times for blood cleansing.
assessments.limitations: 'Blood cleanse' is a traditional concept without a direct clinical equivalent.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Known as Sinkle Bible in Jamaica (washout) and Aloes in Trinidad (cooling); leaf gel is the classic Caribbean burn and skin remedy.

names.name: Sinkle Bible
names.notes: Picking et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Jamaica survey)

names.name: Aloes
names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Trinidad and Tobago survey)

claims.claim: Aloe vera gel aids burn and wound healing

assessments.summary: A review of 23 clinical trials supports Aloe vera as a complementary treatment for burn wound healing.
assessments.population: Burn and wound patients across 23 clinical trials
assessments.main_findings: Evidence supports complementary use for burns.
assessments.limitations: Review-level summary; trial quality not detailed in retrieved record.

claims.claim: Aloes/Sinkle Bible as a washout and cooling remedy

assessments.summary: Washout use documented in Jamaica (54 citations) and cooling use in Trinidad and Tobago (8 citations) in TRAMIL surveys.
assessments.main_findings: Sinkle Bible cited 54 times for washout (Jamaica); aloes cited 8 times for cooling (Trinidad and Tobago).
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy or safety of internal use.

safety.summary: NCCIH notes aloe latex (taken by mouth) carries risks; IARC classifies aloe vera leaf extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans; caution advised in pregnancy.
safety.side_effects: Aloe latex taken orally can cause cramping and diarrhea-type effects.
safety.pregnancy: NCCIH advises caution with aloe use in pregnancy.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Taken up in Jamaican households since the 2000s as teas, juices and food; leaves, pods and seeds are all used.

claims.claim: Moringa supports metabolic health (blood sugar and cholesterol)

assessments.summary: A 2015 review of 5 human studies found anti-hyperglycemic and anti-dyslipidemic effects with no adverse effects reported; studies were small.
assessments.main_findings: Anti-hyperglycemic and anti-dyslipidemic effects; no adverse effects reported.
assessments.limitations: Few, small human studies.
assessments.adverse_effects: No adverse effects reported in the reviewed studies.

assessments.summary: Use in Jamaican households as teas, juices and meals since the 2000s is documented in a peer-reviewed review.
assessments.main_findings: Moringa adopted into Jamaican household use since the 2000s.
assessments.limitations: Documents adoption and use, not clinical efficacy.

safety.summary: No adverse effects reported in the small human studies reviewed by Stohs & Hartman (2015).

plants.traditional_use_summary: Used in Trinidad for cold and cough and in Jamaica for bellyache; ginger tea is a Caribbean household staple.

names.name: Ginger
names.notes: No island-specific name found in retrieved sources; universal name used

claims.claim: Ginger relieves nausea, including nausea in pregnancy

assessments.summary: A 2014 meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (n=1278) found ginger improved nausea but not vomiting significantly; evidence quality was low and no significant safety signal emerged.
assessments.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
assessments.main_findings: Nausea improved; vomiting not significantly reduced.
assessments.limitations: Low-quality evidence overall.
assessments.adverse_effects: No significant safety signal in the reviewed trials.

claims.claim: Ginger for cold, cough and bellyache

assessments.summary: Cold and cough use documented in Trinidad and Tobago (2 citations) and bellyache use in Jamaica (25 citations) in TRAMIL surveys.
assessments.main_findings: Ginger cited for cold & cough (Trinidad) and bellyache (Jamaica, 25 citations).
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Known as saffron/hardi in Trinidad and Tobago, where it is used for afterbirth care; turmeric is also the subject of modern arthritis research.
plants.disambiguation_note: Turmeric is Curcuma longa. In Trinidad it is called 'saffron' (saffron-hardi), not to be confused with true saffron (Crocus sativus).

names.name: Saffron
names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 ('Saffron-hardi')

names.name: Hardi
names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 ('Saffron-hardi')

claims.claim: Turmeric/curcumin alleviates arthritis symptoms

assessments.summary: A 2016 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs found turmeric extracts reduced arthritis pain (VAS -2.04) and WOMAC scores (-15.36); the first author was affiliated with a turmeric supplement manufacturer, which should temper interpretation.
assessments.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
assessments.main_findings: Pain VAS -2.04; WOMAC -15.36.
assessments.limitations: First author affiliated with Daily Manufacturing, Inc. (supplement maker); small evidence base.

claims.claim: Turmeric (saffron-hardi) for afterbirth care

assessments.summary: Afterbirth use documented in the Trinidad and Tobago TRAMIL survey (17 citations).
assessments.main_findings: Saffron-hardi/Curcuma cited 17 times for afterbirth.
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy or safety in the postpartum period.

safety.summary: Welsh NHS information documents turmeric adverse effects including gallstone/biliary concerns, reported liver injury, and bleeding risk.
safety.side_effects: Gallbladder/biliary effects; liver injury has been reported.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Leaf tea used in Trinidad and Tobago for high blood pressure and in Jamaica for nerves; soursop is also widely discussed for its purported anticancer properties.

names.name: Soursop
names.notes: No island-specific name found in retrieved sources; universal name used

distribution.note: POWO native range (tropical Americas); documented use
POWO native range (tropical Americas); documented use

claims.claim: Soursop has anticancer properties

assessments.summary: Anticancer findings are limited to laboratory (in vitro) and animal studies; there are no human trials supporting anticancer use.
assessments.main_findings: Cytotoxic activity observed in preclinical models only.
assessments.limitations: No human evidence; preclinical findings do not establish efficacy in people.

claims.claim: Soursop leaf for high blood pressure and nerves

assessments.summary: HBP use documented in Trinidad and Tobago (8 citations) and use for nerves in Jamaica (83 citations, one of the highest-cited uses in the survey).
assessments.main_findings: Soursop cited 8 times for HBP (Trinidad and Tobago) and 83 times for nerves (Jamaica).
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy.

claims.claim: Soursop fruit/leaves carry a neurotoxicity risk (annonacin)

assessments.summary: Annonacin, found in Annonaceae including soursop, is neurotoxic and has been linked to atypical parkinsonism in Guadeloupe where soursop consumption is high.
assessments.population: Laboratory models; epidemiological link in Guadeloupe
assessments.main_findings: Annonacin is neurotoxic; atypical parkinsonism cluster linked to high Annonaceae consumption in Guadeloupe.
assessments.adverse_effects: Neurotoxicity; atypical parkinsonism risk with heavy chronic consumption.

safety.summary: Heavy chronic consumption of soursop has been linked to atypical parkinsonism via the neurotoxin annonacin (Guadeloupe).

plants.cultural_background: Sorrel drink is a central Jamaican Christmas tradition, made from the dried red calyces with spices.
plants.traditional_use_summary: Sorrel — the red Christmas drink of Jamaica — is also a folk remedy for high blood pressure with clinical trial support.
plants.disambiguation_note: Hibiscus-sorrel here is Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle), the species used for the Caribbean sorrel drink and in medicinal research. It is not the ornamental Hibiscus rosa-sinensis. Note: POWO now places H. sabdariffa as a synonym of Sabdariffa gossypiifolia after the genus Sabdariffa was reinstated (Hibiscus found polyphyletic); the medicinal and TRAMIL literature uniformly uses Hibiscus sabdariffa, retained here.

names.name: Sorrel
names.notes: TopTropicals plant profile (Jamaican Christmas tradition)

names.notes: Widely used English name; no island-specific source retrieved

traditional_uses.use: Folk remedy for high blood pressure

claims.claim: Hibiscus (sorrel) lowers blood pressure

assessments.summary: A 2022 meta-analysis of 17 RCTs found Hibiscus sabdariffa reduced systolic blood pressure by 7.10 mmHg versus placebo.
assessments.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
assessments.population: Adults with elevated blood pressure across 17 RCTs
assessments.main_findings: Systolic BP -7.10 mmHg vs placebo.

assessments.summary: Folk antihypertensive use documented alongside the Jamaican sorrel tradition.
assessments.main_findings: Sorrel documented as a folk remedy for high blood pressure.
assessments.limitations: Documents folk use, not clinical efficacy.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Used in Trinidad and Tobago for diabetes; neem oil is toxic, especially to children, and must never be confused with leaf preparations.

names.name: Neem
names.notes: No island-specific name found in retrieved sources; universal name used

claims.claim: Neem helps manage diabetes

assessments.summary: Use for diabetes documented in the Trinidad and Tobago TRAMIL survey (7 citations). No clinical assessment retrieved for this claim.
assessments.main_findings: Neem cited 7 times for diabetes.
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy; no human trials retrieved.

claims.claim: Neem oil is toxic, especially to children

assessments.summary: A clinical review documents neem oil poisoning, particularly in children: hepatic toxicity, encephalopathy and seizures.
assessments.main_findings: Neem oil poisoning causes hepatic toxicity, encephalopathy and seizures.

safety.summary: Neem oil is toxic and has caused pediatric poisoning (hepatic toxicity, encephalopathy, seizures). Leaf-based traditional preparations are distinct from neem oil.
safety.side_effects: Neem oil: hepatic toxicity, encephalopathy, seizures (especially in children).
safety.children: Neem oil poisoning documented in children; keep neem oil away from children.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Bark traditionally used as a sedative and fish poison in the Caribbean; human evidence is lacking and the plant contains the toxic compound rotenone.
plants.disambiguation_note: Jamaican dogwood (Piscidia piscipula, Fabaceae) is not related to the dogwood family (Cornaceae). It is native to the Caribbean region including Jamaica, Cuba, the Bahamas and Belize.

names.name: Jamaican Dogwood
names.notes: Universal English name referencing Jamaica; no island-specific variant found in retrieved sources

claims.claim: Jamaican dogwood bark works as a sedative / pain remedy

assessments.summary: WebMD states there is no evidence supporting Jamaican dogwood for this use or any other use in humans; the evidence gap is explicitly discussed.
assessments.main_findings: No supporting human evidence identified.
assessments.limitations: Absence of evidence; traditional sedative use is widely claimed but unstudied in humans.

claims.claim: Jamaican dogwood contains rotenone and is toxic

assessments.summary: The plant contains rotenone, a mitochondrial complex I blocker; toxicity includes deaths in poisoning cases and a debated Parkinson's disease link.
assessments.main_findings: Rotenone toxicity documented; deaths reported; Parkinson's risk debated.
assessments.adverse_effects: Rotenone poisoning can be fatal; possible Parkinson's disease link.

safety.summary: Contains rotenone, a mitochondrial poison; deaths have been reported and a Parkinson's disease link is debated. No safe dose is established.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Strong-smelling herb used in Jamaica for headache and in Trinidad and Tobago (as gully root) for cold and cough; studied for anticancer potential but contraindicated in pregnancy.
plants.disambiguation_note: Family placement follows APG IV: Petiveriaceae (older literature places it in Phytolaccaceae). Known as anamu in Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, and mapurite in Trinidad.

names.name: Guinea Hen Weed
names.notes: Picking et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Jamaica survey)

names.name: Gully root
names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Trinidad and Tobago survey)

names.name: Anamu
names.notes: Documented in Caribbean literature (Cuba, Puerto Rico, Dominican Republic)

claims.claim: Guinea hen weed has anticancer properties

assessments.summary: Anticancer findings are limited to a mouse breast-cancer model and related preclinical work; no human trials.
assessments.main_findings: Activity observed in a mouse breast-cancer model.
assessments.limitations: Animal evidence only; no human data.

claims.claim: Guinea hen weed / gully root for headache, cold and cough

assessments.summary: Headache use documented in Jamaica (23 citations) and cold & cough use in Trinidad and Tobago (1 citation) in TRAMIL surveys.
assessments.main_findings: Guinea hen weed cited 23 times for headache (Jamaica); gully root cited once for cold & cough (Trinidad and Tobago).
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy.

claims.claim: Guinea hen weed is unsafe in pregnancy (abortive effect)

assessments.summary: A Costa Rican TRAMIL study attributes an abortive effect to Petiveria alliacea via uterine smooth-muscle contraction; it is contraindicated in pregnancy.
assessments.main_findings: Abortive effect attributed; uterine smooth-muscle contraction documented.

safety.summary: Contraindicated in pregnancy: an abortive effect via uterine smooth-muscle contraction is documented in TRAMIL research.
safety.pregnancy: Contraindicated — abortive effect documented (uterine smooth-muscle contraction).

plants.traditional_use_summary: Breadfruit leaf tea is used in Trinidad and Tobago for high blood pressure; a Jamaican (UWI Mona) animal study found blood-pressure-lowering effects.

names.name: Breadfruit
names.notes: No island-specific name found in retrieved sources; universal name used

claims.claim: Breadfruit leaf lowers blood pressure

assessments.summary: A UWI Mona (Jamaica) study found aqueous breadfruit leaf extract was hypotensive and bradycardic in rats; no human trials retrieved.
assessments.main_findings: Hypotensive and bradycardic effects in rats.
assessments.limitations: Animal evidence only; no human data.

assessments.summary: HBP use documented in the Trinidad and Tobago TRAMIL survey (11 citations).
assessments.main_findings: Breadfruit cited 11 times for HBP.
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Known as Leaf of Life in Jamaica, used for colds; the succulent leaves are also applied to wounds, though the plant contains potentially toxic cardiac glycosides.
plants.disambiguation_note: Wonder-of-the-world is Bryophyllum pinnatum, the name used in Caribbean and TRAMIL literature. POWO accepts Kalanchoe pinnata (Lam.) Pers. with B. pinnatum as a homotypic synonym; both names refer to the same plant. The Commons image is filed under Kalanchoe pinnata and its description notes 'Also known as Bryophyllum pinnatum'.

names.name: Leaf of Life
names.notes: Picking et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Jamaica survey)

names.name: Kalanchoe pinnata
names.notes: Accepted name on POWO; homotypic synonym

names.name: Wonder of the World
names.notes: Widely used Caribbean English name; no island-specific source retrieved

claims.claim: Leaf of Life aids wound healing

assessments.summary: Preclinical (animal/laboratory) studies provide the most extensive evidence for wound-healing effects; no human trials retrieved.
assessments.preparation_studied: Kalanchoe pinnata / Bryophyllum pinnatum leaf preparations
assessments.main_findings: Wound-healing effects in preclinical models.
assessments.limitations: No human evidence.

claims.claim: Leaf of Life for colds

assessments.summary: Cold use documented in the Jamaican TRAMIL survey (51 citations).
assessments.main_findings: Leaf of Life cited 51 times for cold.
assessments.limitations: Survey data document use, not efficacy.

claims.claim: Wonder-of-the-world contains toxic cardiac glycosides (bufadienolides)

assessments.summary: The plant contains bufadienolides, cardiac-glycoside compounds with poisoning risk if ingested in quantity.
assessments.main_findings: Bufadienolides documented; cardiac-glycoside poisoning risk.

safety.summary: Contains bufadienolides (cardiac glycosides); poisoning risk if ingested in quantity.

plants.traditional_use_summary: Passion fruit leaf documented in Trinidad and Tobago for high blood pressure; Brazilian tradition and a mouse study point to calming effects.
plants.disambiguation_note: Passionflower here is Passiflora edulis Sims, the species documented in the Trinidad TRAMIL survey ('Passion fruit', HBP, 1 cite). P. incarnata was rejected: it is native only to the southeastern USA with no Caribbean distribution on POWO. P. quadrangularis ('Barbadine', HBP, 9 cites in the same survey) is a related but distinct species not covered by this record.

names.name: Passion fruit
names.notes: Clement et al. 2015 (TRAMIL Trinidad and Tobago survey, as Passiflora edulis)

claims.claim: Passionflower leaf has calming / anxiolytic effects

assessments.summary: Aqueous P. edulis leaf extract showed anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects in mice; traditional Brazilian use for anxiety and insomnia is noted. No human trials retrieved.
assessments.main_findings: Anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects in mice.
assessments.limitations: Animal evidence only; no human data.

assessments.summary: HBP use documented in the Trinidad and Tobago TRAMIL survey (1 citation); Brazilian traditional use for anxiety/insomnia noted in the pharmacological literature.
assessments.main_findings: Passion fruit/P. edulis cited once for HBP.
assessments.limitations: Single citation; survey data document use, not efficacy.
